title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Seven years had passed. The storm-tossed sea of European history had settled back within its shores and seemed to have grown calm. But the mysterious forces that move humanity—mysterious because the laws governing their motion are unknown to us—went on working.

Though the surface of the sea of history looked motionless, the movement of humanity went on just as unceasingly as the flow of time itself. Various groups of people formed and dissolved; the coming formation and dissolution of kingdoms, and the displacement of whole peoples, was quietly being prepared.

The sea of history was no longer being driven spasmodically from shore to shore the way it had been before. Now it was seething in its depths. Historical figures were no longer being carried by the waves from one shore to another, as they had been. Now they seemed to spin in place. The historical figures who stood at the head of armies, and who had once reflected the movement of the masses by ordering wars, campaigns, and battles, now reflected that same restless movement through political and diplomatic maneuvering, laws, and treaties.
Historians call this activity on the part of historical figures "the reaction."

All the well-known people of that era—from Alexander and Napoleon down to the writer Madame de Staël, the churchman Photius, the philosophers Schelling and Fichte, and the writer Chateaubriand, and the rest—are marched before their severe tribunal and either acquitted or condemned, depending on whether they are judged to have served progress or reaction.

According to these accounts, a reaction took place in Russia too at that time, and the chief culprit, they say, was Alexander I—the very same man who, by their own account, had been the chief cause of the liberal movement at the start of his reign, and the savior of Russia besides.

There is no one left in Russian letters today, from schoolboy essayist to learned historian, who doesn't throw his own little stone at Alexander for what he did wrong during this stretch of his reign.

"He should have acted this way here, and that way there. In this instance he did well, in that instance badly. He behaved admirably at the start of his reign and during 1812, but he behaved badly by granting Poland a constitution, by forming the Holy Alliance, by handing power over to his minister Arakcheev, by favoring Golitsyn and his mysticism, and later the statesman Shishkov and Photius. He also behaved badly by meddling in the affairs of the active army, and by disbanding the Semyonov regiment, an elite guards unit."
It would take a dozen pages to list every single reproach the historians level at him, all of it drawn from their own certainty about what is good for humanity.
What do these reproaches actually mean?

Don't the very same actions the historians praise Alexander I for—his liberal moves at the start of his reign, his struggle against Napoleon, the firmness he showed in 1812 and in the campaign of 1813—flow from the very same sources? Those sources are the circumstances of his birth, his upbringing, his life, the things that made him the man he was. And isn't it from those same sources that the actions they blame him for also flowed—the Holy Alliance, the restoration of Poland, the reaction of 1820 and after?
So what does the substance of these reproaches actually come down to?

It comes down to this. A historical figure like Alexander I stands on the very highest peak of human power, with the blinding light of history trained on him. He is a man exposed to the strongest influences there are—the intrigue, the flattery, the self-deception that power inevitably brings with it. He is a man who at every single moment of his life felt himself responsible for everything happening across Europe. And he is a living man, not some invented character, a man who like every other man had his own personal habits, passions, impulses toward goodness, beauty, and truth. For all his undoubted virtue—even the historians don't deny him that—this man simply did not hold the same idea of what was good for humanity fifty years ago that a present-day professor holds, a professor who has spent his whole life since youth doing nothing but study, which is to say, reading books and lectures and taking notes on them.

But even granting that Alexander I was mistaken, fifty years ago, in his view of what was good for the people, we're forced to assume something else as well. The historian sitting in judgment on Alexander will, after enough time has passed, turn out to have been just as mistaken in his own view of what's good for humanity. This assumption isn't just natural, it's unavoidable, because if you watch the movement of history, you see that opinion about what's good for mankind shifts every year, with every new writer, so that what looked good ten years ago looks bad now, and the reverse. What's more, we find flatly contradictory views held at one and the same time about what counts as good and bad in history: some people count granting Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance as praiseworthy acts of Alexander's, while others count the very same acts as blameworthy.

The activity of Alexander, or of Napoleon, can't rightly be called either useful or harmful, because there's no way to say what, exactly, it was useful or harmful for. If that activity displeases someone, it's only because it doesn't line up with that person's own limited idea of what's good. I might judge the preservation of my father's house in Moscow, the glory of Russian arms, the prosperity of the universities of Petersburg and elsewhere, the freedom of Poland, the greatness of Russia, the balance of power in Europe, or some particular kind of European culture called "progress" to be good or bad. But whichever way I judge it, I have to admit that beyond all these things, the actions of every historical figure serve other, more general purposes that I simply cannot see.

But let's grant, for argument's sake, that what we call science can reconcile all these contradictions and does possess some fixed, unchanging standard of good and bad by which to judge historical figures and events. Let's say Alexander could have done everything differently. Let's say that, guided by the very people who blame him now—people who claim to know the ultimate goal humanity is moving toward—he could have arranged everything according to the program his present-day accusers would hand him: nationality, freedom, equality, progress. Let's say that about covers it. Let's assume this program was achievable, that it had already been worked out at the time, and that Alexander had acted on it. What, then, would have become of the activity of everyone who opposed the government's prevailing policy at that time—activity that the historians themselves judge to have been good and beneficial? That activity simply would not have existed. There would have been no life at all. There would have been nothing.
If we accept that human life can be governed by reason, then the very possibility of life is destroyed.
